steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on a graph-based recommender system that works when user interaction data is small, sparse and heterogeneous. Motivate the small-data problem, review the usual remedies and their limits, and introduce our approach and how we evaluate it.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
With the internet, huge amounts of data have become available. This makes it possible to design and develop new Recommender Systems (RSs) based on complex Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) approaches, which are often described as data-hungry. Many recent recommender models are in this category, so a recommender dataset of size 100 K might already be considered small. Also, when these datasets are used, a pre-processing step is often applied that removes all users with less than a certain number of interactions, e.g., 5, because several models cannot learn with only a few data points per user.

In the era of big data, Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) struggle, because they might not have access to such huge amounts of data. But SMEs are fundamental actors in the global economy: they represent about 90\% of businesses and more than 50\% of employment worldwide. In these cases RSs that can cope with low data scenarios are needed.

Small data problems are notoriously hard in ML and DL, and they are usually solved with a number of well-studied techniques: (1) data augmentation, where synthetic samples are generated from the training set; (2) transfer learning, where models learn from a related task and then transfer the knowledge; (3) self supervision, where models learn from pseudo or weak labels; (4) few-shot learning, i.e., (meta-)learning from many related tasks with the aim of improving the performance on the problem of interest; (5) exploiting prior knowledge that is manually encoded, for example external side information and Knowledge Graphs (KGs). But apart from hand-coded knowledge, these approaches still need a considerable amount of initial data, or access to a different but similar domain where there is plenty of data. Knowledge bases on the other hand are application dependent, need access to expert knowledge, and are not always available.

- Our approach: heterogeneous graph + PPR with learned edge weights
  - novel recommender for small data; no large initial data; not application dependent
  - heterogeneous graph: vertices = entities (users, content types); edges = user-content interactions (e.g., posting a message on social media)
  - Personalized PageRank (PPR) to recommend items
  - edges: any interaction, not only with recommendable items
  - edge weights = strength of user-content relationship; usually pre-defined per application in prior RS work
  - no assumption on weights; optimized with a genetic algorithm
  - to our knowledge, heuristic algorithms never used to learn edge weights in RSs

- Evaluation on two real-world use cases
  - (1) emergent educational social network: few interactions (initial stage of platform), many items
  - (2) insurance e-commerce platform: many users, few interactions (rare interaction with insurance products), few items by nature of domain
  - promising results: up to 7\% improvement over state-of-the-art baselines

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
With the internet, huge amounts of data have become available. This makes it possible to design and develop new Recommender Systems (RSs) based on complex Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) approaches, which are often described as data-hungry. Many recent recommender models are in this category, so a recommender dataset of size 100 K might already be considered small. Also, when these datasets are used, a pre-processing step is often applied that removes all users with less than a certain number of interactions, e.g., 5, because several models cannot learn with only a few data points per user.

In the era of big data, Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) struggle, because they might not have access to such huge amounts of data. But SMEs are fundamental actors in the global economy: they represent about 90\% of businesses and more than 50\% of employment worldwide. In these cases RSs that can cope with low data scenarios are needed.

Small data problems are notoriously hard in ML and DL, and they are usually solved with a number of well-studied techniques: (1) data augmentation, where synthetic samples are generated from the training set; (2) transfer learning, where models learn from a related task and then transfer the knowledge; (3) self supervision, where models learn from pseudo or weak labels; (4) few-shot learning, i.e., (meta-)learning from many related tasks with the aim of improving the performance on the problem of interest; (5) exploiting prior knowledge that is manually encoded, for example external side information and Knowledge Graphs (KGs). But apart from hand-coded knowledge, these approaches still need a considerable amount of initial data, or access to a different but similar domain where there is plenty of data. Knowledge bases on the other hand are application dependent, need access to expert knowledge, and are not always available.

In this paper we contribute a new recommender approach that can operate in small data scenarios: our model does not need large volumes of initial data and it is not application dependent. We use a heterogeneous graph, where the vertices are entities, e.g., users and different types of content, and the edges are interactions between users and content, e.g., a user posting a message on a social media. Then we use Personalized PageRank (PPR) to recommend items. The edges represent any interaction with users and content, not only interactions with recommendable items. We assign weights to the edges of the graph, and these represent how strong the relationship between users and content is. In previous work within RSs these weights are usually pre-defined depending on the application. We do not make any assumption on the values of the weights, and we optimize them with a genetic algorithm. As far as we know, heuristic algorithms have never been applied to learn edge weights in the context of RSs.

We evaluate our approach on two real-world use cases. The first is an emergent educational social network, where there are few user interactions because the platform is at an initial stage, but there is a large number of items. The second is an insurance e-commerce platform, where there are many users but few user interactions, because users do not interact often with insurance products, and there are few items by the nature of the insurance domain. The experimental results are promising and show up to a 7\% improvement over state-of-the-art baselines.

steps.text:

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
With the internet, huge amounts of data have become available. This allows to design and develop novel Recommender Systems (RSs) based on complex Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) approaches, often described as data-hungry approaches. Many recent recommender models belong to this category, so a recommender dataset of size 100 K might already be considered small [1]. Moreover, when using such datasets, a pre-processing step is often applied to remove all users with less than a certain number of interactions, e.g., 5, because several models are not able to learn with only few data points per user [2,3,4,5].

In the era of big data, Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) struggle to find their way, since they might not have access to such a huge amount of data. However, SMEs are fundamental actors in the global economy, as they represent about 90\% of businesses and more than 50\% of employment worldwide [6]. In these cases, RSs able to cope with low data scenarios are necessary [7].

In ML and DL, small data problems are notoriously hard and they are usually solved with a number of well-studied techniques [8]: (1) data augmentation, where synthetic samples are generated from the training set [9,10,11]; (2) transfer learning, where models learn from a related task and transfer the knowledge [12,13]; (3) self supervision, where models learns from pseudo or weak labels [14,15]; (4) few-shot learning, i.e., (meta-)learning from many related tasks with the aim of improving the performance on the problem of interest [16,17,18]; (5) exploiting prior knowledge manually encoded, for example external side information and Knowledge Graphs (KGs) [19,20]. However, apart from hand-coded knowledge, these approaches still require a considerable amount of initial data or access to a different, but similar domain, where plenty of data is available. On the other side, knowledge bases are application dependent, require access to expert knowledge, and are not always available.

In this paper, we contribute a novel recommender approach able to operate in small data scenarios: our model does not require large volumes of initial data and is not application dependent. We use a heterogeneous graph, where vertices denote entities, e.g., users and different types of content, and edges represent interactions between users and content, e.g., a user posting a message on a social media. Then we use Personalized PageRank (PPR) to recommend items. Edges represent any interaction with users and content, not only interaction with recommendable items. We assign weights to edges in the graph, which represent the strength of the relationship between users and content. In previous work within RSs [21,22,23], such weights are usually pre-defined depending on the application. We do not make any assumption on the values of such weights and optimize them with a genetic algorithm [24]. As far as we know, heuristic algorithms have never been applied to learn edge weights in the context of RSs. Our approach is evaluated on two real-world use cases: (1) an emergent educational social network, where there are few user interactions due to the initial stage of the platform, but a large number of items; (2) an insurance e-commerce platform, where there are many users but few user interactions, because users do not interact often with insurance products, and few items by nature of the insurance domain. Experimental results are promising and show up to a 7\% improvement over state-of-the-art baselines.
